'''Eric Oldfield''' (born 1948) is an [[English people|English]] [[chemist]], the Harriet A. Harlin [[professor]] of [[chemistry]] and a professor of [[biophysics]] at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://chemistry.illinois.edu/eoldfiel|title=Eric Oldfield &#124; Chemistry at Illinois|website=chemistry.illinois.edu}}</ref> He is known for his work in [[nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy]] of [[lipids]], [[proteins]] and [[membranes]]; of inorganic solids; in [[computational chemistry]], and in [[microbiology]] and [[parasitology]]. He has received a number of recognitions for his work, including the [[ACS Award in Pure Chemistry|American Chemical Society's Award in Pure Chemistry]], the [[Meldola Medal and Prize|Royal Society of Chemistry's Meldola Medal]] and the [[Colworth Medal|Biochemical Society's Colworth Medal]]. He is a member of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] and a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].

==Early life and education==
Oldfield was born in [[London]], England on 23 May 1948. He attended [[Bristol University]] doing research with [[Jake MacMillan]] on [[diterpene]]s and [[Geoffrey Eglinton]] on lipids and isoprenoids. He graduated with a Bachelor of Science degree in 1969. He obtained a PhD in [[biophysical chemistry]] from the [[University of Sheffield]] in 1972, with Dennis Chapman, developing [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] methods to study lipid and membrane structure. He worked as a Research Associate and EMBO Postdoctoral Fellow at [[Indiana University]] with Adam Allerhand, on the development of high-resolution NMR of proteins (1972–1974)<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0022-2364%2873%2990013-9|title=Carbon-13 fourier transform nmr at 14.2 kg in a 20 mm probe|first1=Adam|last1=Allerhand|first2=RayF|last2=Childers|first3=Eric|last3=Oldfield|date=August 1, 1973|journal=Journal of Magnetic Resonance|volume=11|issue=2|pages=272–278|via=ScienceDirect|doi=10.1016/0022-2364(73)90013-9|bibcode=1973JMagR..11..272A |url-access=subscription}}</ref> and was then a Visiting Scientist at MIT with [[John S. Waugh]] (1974-1975), working on solid-state NMR.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://academictree.org/chemistry/peopleinfo.php?pid=13674|title=Chemistry Tree - John S. Waugh|website=academictree.org}}</ref>

==Career==
Oldfield joined the Department of Chemistry at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1975 as an assistant Professor of Chemistry. He was promoted to associate professor in 1980 and was a Professor from 1982 to 2002. He was then an Alumni Research Professor of Chemistry from 2003 to 2013 and since then has been the Harriet A. Harlin Professor of Chemistry. He has also been a professor of biophysics in the Center for Computational Biology and Biophysics since 1995 and was a Fellow in the Center for Advanced Study in 1979, a Richard G. and Carole J. Cline University Senior Scholar in 1995 and an Associate in the Center for Advanced Study in 2000. He has authored 450 publications and as of 2023, has an h-index of 104 with 35,000 citations, according to Google Scholar<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=CHko4c8AAAAJ&hl=en|title=Eric Oldfield|website=scholar.google.com}}</ref> and holds nine issued [[patent]]s from the [[United States Patent and Trademark Office]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://patents.justia.com/inventor/eric-oldfield|title=Eric Oldfield Inventions, Patents and Patent Applications – Justia Patents Search|website=patents.justia.com}}</ref>

==Research==
{{multiple issues|{{Excessive citations|date=June 2026|section}}{{Overly detailed|Section|nosplit=nosplit|date=June 2026}}|section=y{{Cleanup rewrite|date=June 2026}}
}}
Oldfield is known for his research in nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and [[drug discovery]]. His invention of [[deuterium]] and [[proton]] NMR methods led to new ways to study the structures of lipids and membranes; his carbon-13 NMR and quantum chemical developments led to new ways to investigate [[protein structure]]s; his investigations of quadrupolar nuclei led to new research in [[materials science]], [[geochemistry]] and [[catalysis]], and his more recent research using NMR, computational and [[crystallography|crystallographic methods]] has led to the development of new therapeutic approaches to treating both [[infection|infectious diseases]] and [[cancer]], targeting [[Lipid metabolism|lipid biosynthesis]].

===NMR of lipids and membranes===
In the 1970s and 1980s Oldfield developed ways to investigate lipid and membrane structure including the use of 2H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy of labelled compounds.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/82634005.pdf| title=deuteron resonance:A novel approach to the study of hydrocarbon chain mobility in membrane systems}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/bi00607a006|title=Spectroscopic studies of specifically deuterium labeled membrane systems. Nuclear magnetic resonance investigation of the effects of cholesterol in model systems|first1=Eric|last1=Oldfield|first2=Michael|last2=Meadows|first3=David|last3=Rice|first4=Russell|last4=Jacobs|date=July 11, 1978|journal=Biochemistry|volume=17|issue=14|pages=2727–2740|doi=10.1021/bi00607a006|pmid=687560 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> This method enabled the determination of the static and dynamic structures of lipids, and how they interact with proteins and sterol molecules such as cholesterol.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/quarterly-reviews-of-biophysics/article/abs/deuterium-magnetic-resonance-theory-and-application-to-lipid-membranes/A6C891724A6AE72FF2395F3549042D75| title= Deuterium magnetic resonance: theory and application to lipid membranes | date= 1977 | doi= 10.1017/S0033583500002948 | last1= Seelig | first1= Joachim | journal= Quarterly Reviews of Biophysics | volume= 10 | issue= 3 | pages= 353–418 | pmid= 335428 | bibcode= 1977QRBio..10..353S | s2cid= 33372264 | url-access= subscription }}</ref> In addition, he developed 1H and 13C magic-angle sample-spinning methods to investigate lipid membranes without the need for isotopic labeling. The magic-angle technique was not thought to be applicable to 1H NMR (due to strong dipolar interactions), but he showed that due to fast axial diffusion, these interactions were scaled and that remarkably high-resolution spectra could be obtained.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/1988/f1/f19888403821| title= Some new developments in solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopic studies of lipids and biological membranes, including the effects of cholesterol in model and natural systems | date= 1988 | doi= 10.1039/F19888403821 | last1= Forbes | first1= Jeffrey | last2= Bowers | first2= John | last3= Shan | first3= Xi | last4= Moran | first4= Liam | last5= Oldfield | first5= Eric | last6= Moscarello | first6= Mario A. | journal= Journal of the Chemical Society, Faraday Transactions 1: Physical Chemistry in Condensed Phases | volume= 84 | issue= 11 | page= 3821 | url-access= subscription }}</ref>

===NMR of proteins===
In the early 1970s, while working with Adam Allerhand, Oldfield reported the first high-resolution 13C NMR spectra of proteins—lysozyme, myoglobin and cytochrome c—in which numerous single carbon atom sites could be resolved and assigned.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/bi00731a013| title=Natural-abundance carbon-13 nuclear magnetic resonance studies in 20-mm sample tubes. Numerous single-carbon resonances of hen egg-white lysozyme | year=1973 | doi=10.1021/bi00731a013 | last1=Allerhand | first1=Adam | last2=Childres | first2=Ray F. | last3=Oldfield | first3=Eric | journal=Biochemistry | volume=12 | issue=7 | pages=1335–1341 | pmid=4735301 | url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal| title=Cytochrome c. Observation of Numerous Single-Carbon Sites of the Reduced and Oxidized Species by Means of Natural-Abundance 13C Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy| year=1973| doi=10.1073/pnas.70.12.3531| last1=Oldfield| first1=Eric| last2=Allerhand| first2=Adam| journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences| volume=70| issue=12| pages=3531–3535| pmid=4357878| pmc=427274| doi-access=free}}</ref> The origins of the chemical shift non-equivalencies observed due to folding remained unexplained until 1993 when he showed that 13C and 15N chemical shifts in proteins could be well predicted by using quantum chemical methods. He reasoned that since the chemical shift is essentially a local phenomenon, it might be possible to compute chemical shifts just by using small peptide fragments and a "locally dense" basis set, and this turned out to be correct.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.8502992| title=Secondary and Tertiary Structural Effects on Protein NMR Chemical Shifts: an ab Initio Approach | year=1993 | doi=10.1126/science.8502992 | last1=De Dios | first1=Angel C. | last2=Pearson | first2=John G. | last3=Oldfield | first3=Eric | journal=Science | volume=260 | issue=5113 | pages=1491–1496 | pmid=8502992 | bibcode=1993Sci...260.1491D | url-access=subscription }}</ref> His early work also led to the demonstration that computed chemical shift tensors could be used in protein structure refinement.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Protein Structure Refinement Using 13 Cα Chemical Shift Tensors|first1=Benjamin J.|last1=Wylie|first2=Charles D.|last2=Schwieters|first3=Eric|last3=Oldfield|first4=Chad M.|last4=Rienstra|date=January 28, 2009|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=131|issue=3|pages=985–992|doi=10.1021/ja804041p|pmid=19123862|pmc=2751586|bibcode=2009JAChS.131..985W }}</ref> Moreover, he showed that the chemical shifts of non-native species in proteins such as 19F nuclei, could be also be computed, and were due to electric field effects.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/ja00068a049| title= Chemical shifts in proteins: a shielding trajectory analysis of the fluorine nuclear magnetic resonance spectrum of the Escherichia coli galactose binding protein using a multipole shielding polarizability-local reaction field-molecular dynamics approach | year= 1993 | doi= 10.1021/ja00068a049 | last1= Pearson | first1= John G. | last2= Oldfield | first2= Eric | last3= Lee | first3= Frederick S. | last4= Warshel | first4= Arieh | journal= Journal of the American Chemical Society | volume= 115 | issue= 15 | pages= 6851–6862 | bibcode= 1993JAChS.115.6851P | url-access= subscription }}</ref>

===NMR inorganic solids===
Oldfield began to investigate structures of a variety of inorganic solids in the 1980s. He showed that high-resolution spectra of quadrupolar nuclei (such as 17O, 23Na) could be obtained by using variable-angle sample-spinning,<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/abs/10.1063/1.444436 | title= Variable-angle sample-spinning high resolution NMR of solids| year= 1982| doi= 10.1063/1.444436| last1= Ganapathy| first1= Subramanian| last2= Schramm| first2= Suzanne| last3= Oldfield| first3= Eric| journal= The Journal of Chemical Physics| volume= 77| issue= 9| pages= 4360–4365| url-access= subscription}}</ref> spin echo,<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0022236486902246| title=Solid-state spin-echo Fourier transform NMR of 39K and 67Zn salts at high field | date=1986 | doi=10.1016/0022-2364(86)90224-6 | last1=Kunwar | first1=A.C | last2=Turner | first2=Gary L. | last3=Oldfield | first3=Eric | journal=Journal of Magnetic Resonance | volume=69 | pages=124–127 | url-access=subscription }}</ref> as well as spectral deconvolution methods.<ref>{{cite journal|url= https://www.nature.com/articles/318163a0| title= High-resolution solid-state NMR of quadrupolar nuclei| date= 1985| doi= 10.1038/318163a0| last1= Oldfield| first1= Eric| last2= Timken| first2= Hye Kyung C.| last3= Montez| first3= Ben| last4= Ramachandran| first4= R.| journal= Nature| volume= 318| issue= 6042| pages= 163–165| bibcode= 1985Natur.318..163O| s2cid= 4329616| url-access= subscription}}</ref> In his collaborative research with R. James Kirkpatrick, he investigated the 29Si magic-angle sample-spinning NMR spectra of a wide range of natural and synthetic silicates,<ref>{{cite journal|url= https://pubs.geoscienceworld.org/msa/ammin/article-abstract/68/11-12/1206/104801/High-resolution-silicon-29-nuclear-magnetic| title= High-resolution silicon-29 nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopic study of rock-forming silicates  | journal= American Mineralogist | date= December 1983 | volume= 68 | issue= 11–12 | pages= 1206–1215 | last1= Smith | first1= Karen Ann | last2= Kirkpatrick | first2= R. James | last3= Oldfield | first3= Eric | last4= Henderson | first4= Donald M. }}</ref> showing that both Si-O bond length-chemical shift and bond strength-chemical shift relationships were useful tools for investigating the structures of crystalline silicates and, more importantly, silicate glasses, clays and zeolites that cannot be examined by single crystal X-ray or neutron diffraction methods. He also worked on investigating Pt/Ru direct methanol oxidation fuel cell catalysts using 13C and 195Pt NMR, in collaboration with A. Wieckowksi, which clarified the mechanism of enhanced CO tolerance in Pt/Ru versus pure Pt catalysts.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/0-306-47927-3_1|title=Modern Aspects of Electrochemistry No. 36|first1=P. K.|last1=Babu|first2=E.|last2=Oldfield|first3=A.|last3=Wieckowski|editor-first1=C. G.|editor-last1=Vayenas|editor-first2=B. E.|editor-last2=Conway|editor-first3=Ralph E.|editor-last3=White|editor-first4=Maria E.|editor-last4=Gamboa-Adelco|date=March 17, 2003|publisher=Springer US|pages=1–50|via=Springer Link|doi=10.1007/0-306-47927-3_1}}</ref>

===Antibiotics===
In 1999, Oldfield shifted his research to more biomedical applications. Working in collaboration with Julio Urbina and Roberto Docampo, his group found, using 31P NMR spectroscopy, that the parasitic protozoan ''[[Trypanosoma cruzi]]'', the causative agent of [[Chagas disease]], contained very high levels of diphosphate, and that diphosphate analogs, [[bisphosphonate]]s used clinically to treat bone resorption diseases, killed these parasites.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Trypanosoma cruzi Contains Major Pyrophosphate Stores, and Its Growth in Vitro and in Vivo Is Blocked by Pyrophosphate Analogs *|first1=Julio A.|last1=Urbina|first2=Benjamin|last2=Moreno|first3=Stephanie|last3=Vierkotter|first4=Eric|last4=Oldfield|first5=Gilberto|last5=Payares|first6=Cristina|last6=Sanoja|first7=Brian N.|last7=Bailey|first8=Wen|last8=Yan|first9=David A.|last9=Scott|first10=Silvia N. J.|last10=Moreno|first11=Roberto|last11=Docampo|date=November 19, 1999|journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry|volume=274|issue=47|pages=33609–33615|doi=10.1074/jbc.274.47.33609|pmid=10559249|doi-access=free }}</ref> as well as others.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/jm0002578|title=Bisphosphonates Inhibit the Growth of ''Trypanosoma brucei'', ''Trypanosoma cruzi'', ''Leishmania d onovani'', ''Toxoplasma g ondii'', and ''Plasmodium f alciparum'' : A Potential Route to Chemotherapy|first1=Michael B.|last1=Martin|first2=Joshua S.|last2=Grimley|first3=Jared C.|last3=Lewis|first4=Huel T.|last4=Heath|first5=Brian N.|last5=Bailey|first6=Howard|last6=Kendrick|first7=Vanessa|last7=Yardley|first8=Aura|last8=Caldera|first9=Renee|last9=Lira|first10=Julio A.|last10=Urbina|first11=Silvia N. J.|last11=Moreno|first12=Roberto|last12=Docampo|first13=Simon L.|last13=Croft|first14=Eric|last14=Oldfield|date=March 1, 2001|journal=Journal of Medicinal Chemistry|volume=44|issue=6|pages=909–916|doi=10.1021/jm0002578|pmid=11300872 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> He also discovered that the bisphosphonate pamidronate cured mice of leishmaniasis<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://academic.oup.com/jid/article/186/1/138/837343|title=Radical Cure of Experimental Cutaneous Leishmaniasis by the Bisphosphonate Pamidronate |date=2002 |doi=10.1086/341074 |last1=Rodriguez |first1=Noris |last2=Bailey |first2=Brian N. |last3=Martin |first3=Michael B. |last4=Oldfield |first4=Eric |last5=Urbina |first5=Julio A. |last6=Docampo |first6=Roberto |journal=The Journal of Infectious Diseases |volume=186 |issue=1 |pages=138–140 |pmid=12089677 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> and proposed that farnesyl diphosphate synthase (FPPS) can be used as the target of bisphosphonate drugs<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0006291X99914043| title=Nitrogen-Containing Bisphosphonates as Carbocation Transition State Analogs for Isoprenoid Biosynthesis | date=1999 | doi=10.1006/bbrc.1999.1404 | last1=Martin | first1=Michael B. | last2=Arnold | first2=William | last3=Heath | first3=Huel T. | last4=Urbina | first4=Julio A. | last5=Oldfield | first5=Eric | journal=Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications | volume=263 | issue=3 | pages=754–758 | pmid=10512752 | bibcode=1999BBRC..263..754M | url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Oldfield then discovered another compound that killed ''T. cruzi'', the antiarrhythmic drug amiodarone, and that it acted synergistically with the azole drug posaconazole.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/jm050691f | title= Amiodarone Has Intrinsic Anti-Trypanosoma cruzi Activity and Acts Synergistically with posaconazole†| year= 2006| doi= 10.1021/jm050691f| last1= Benaim| first1= Gustavo| last2= Sanders| first2= John M.| last3= Garcia-Marchán| first3= Yael| last4= Colina| first4= Claudia| last5= Lira| first5= Renee| last6= Caldera| first6= Aura R.| last7= Payares| first7= Gilberto| last8= Sanoja| first8= Cristina| last9= Burgos| first9= Juan Miguel| last10= Leon-Rossell| first10= Annette| last11= Concepcion| first11= Juan Luis| last12= Schijman| first12= Alejandro G.| last13= Levin| first13= Mariano| last14= Oldfield| first14= Eric| last15= Urbina| first15= Julio A.| journal= Journal of Medicinal Chemistry| volume= 49| issue= 3| pages= 892–899| pmid= 16451055| hdl= 11336/79898| hdl-access= free}}</ref>  He then began to investigate antibacterial agents. ===Anti-cancer drug leads===
In 2012, Oldfield's group synthesized lipophilic analogs of the clinical bisphosphonate drugs zoledronate and risedronate, to prevent unwanted binding to bone mineral, and found they had potent anti-malarial activity.<ref>{{cite journal| title=Lipophilic analogs of zoledronate and risedronate inhibit Plasmodium geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase (GGPPS) and exhibit potent antimalarial ===Isoprenoid synthesis===
Oldfield and his collaborators have reported the structures and mechanisms of action of many proteins involved in isoprenoid biosynthesis, focusing on the modular structures found.<ref>{{cite journal| title=Terpene Biosynthesis: Modularity Rules | year=2012 | doi=10.1002/anie.201103110 | last1=Oldfield | first1=Eric | last2=Lin | first2=Fu-Yang | journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition | volume=51 | issue=5 | pages=1124–1137 | pmid=22105807 | pmc=3769779 | bibcode=2012ACIE...51.1124O }}</ref> They successfully predicted the αβγ tri-domain found in diterpene cyclases.<ref>{{cite journal| title=Diterpene cyclases and the nature of the isoprene fold | year=2010 | doi=10.1002/prot.22751 | last1=Cao | first1=Rong | last2=Zhang | first2=Yonghui | last3=Mann | first3=Francis M. | last4=Huang | first4=Cancan | last5=Mukkamala | first5=Dushyant | last6=Hudock | first6=Michael P. | last7=Mead | first7=Matthew E. | last8=Prisic | first8=Sladjana | last9=Wang | first9=Ke | last10=Lin | first10=Fu-Yang | last11=Chang | first11=Ting-Kai | last12=Peters | first12=Reuben J. | last13=Oldfield | first13=Eric | journal=Proteins: Structure, Function, and Bioinformatics | volume=78 | issue=11 | pages=2417–2432 | pmid=20602361 | pmc=3805035 }}</ref> Furthermore, they used electron paramagnetic resonance and X-ray crystallography to develop the organometallic mechanism of action of the unusual 4Fe-4S proteins IspG and IspH involved in the early stages of isoprenoid biosynthesis,<ref>{{cite journal| title=Bioorganometallic Chemistry with IspG and IspH: Structure, Function, and Inhibition of the [Fe4S4] Proteins Involved in Isoprenoid Biosynthesis | year=2014 | doi=10.1002/anie.201306712 | last1=Wang | first1=Weixue | last2=Oldfield | first2=Eric | journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition | volume=53 | issue=17 | pages=4294–4310 | pmid=24481599 | pmc=3997630 | bibcode=2014ACIE...53.4294W }}</ref> and also used X-ray methods for providing mechanisms of action for the terpene cyclases.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/acscatal.0c04710| title=Terpene Cyclases and Prenyltransferases: Structures and Mechanisms of Action| year=2021| doi=10.1021/acscatal.0c04710| last1=Chen| first1=Chun-Chi| last2=Malwal| first2=Satish R.| last3=Han| first3=Xu| last4=Liu| first4=Weidong| last5=Ma| first5=Lixin| last6=Zhai|
